  • If it enters perpendicular to the field, it follows a parabolic path, exactly like a projectile under gravity: uniform motion along its original direction combined with uniformly accelerated motion along the field.
  • The deflection after travelling a length L at speed v is:

y = (1/2) (q E / m) (L / v)2

  • A positive charge is deflected towards the negative plate; a negative charge (such as an electron) towards the positive plate.
  • This principle is used in cathode-ray tubes and inkjet printers.

lessons.title: Electric Current and Drift Velocity
lessons.notes_html:
A steady current is a current whose magnitude and direction do not change with time. Current is the rate of flow of charge:

I = Q / t

  • The conventional direction of current is the direction of flow of positive charge — from the positive terminal to the negative terminal outside the source — opposite to the actual flow of electrons.
  • Sources of current maintain a potential difference: cells and batteries (chemical energy), generators (mechanical energy), solar cells (light energy) and thermocouples (heat energy).

Drift of Free Electrons

In a metal, free electrons move randomly at high speed with no net flow. When a potential difference is applied, a small drift velocity is added to this random motion, opposite to the field direction (electrons are negative). This slow, steady drift of the whole electron gas — typically only millimetres per second — is the electric current.

Current in Electrolytes and Plasmas

In an electrolyte or a plasma, current is carried by ions, not electrons alone: positive ions (cations) drift towards the cathode and negative ions (anions) towards the anode, and both streams contribute to the current. In a plasma, free electrons and positive ions both carry the current.

lessons.title: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
lessons.notes_html:
Ohm's Law

At constant temperature, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it:

V = I R

  • R — resistance of the conductor, in ohms (Ω)
  • Ohmic materials obey the law: their V-I graph is a straight line through the origin (metals at constant temperature).
  • Non-ohmic materials do not: filament lamps (resistance rises as the filament heats), diodes (current flows mainly one way) and thermistors.

Resistivity and Conductivity

R = ρ L / A

  • ρ — resistivity: the resistance of a 1 m cube of the material, unit Ω m. It depends on the material and its temperature, not on the shape of the sample.
  • Doubling the length of a wire doubles its resistance; doubling the area halves it.
  • Conductivity σ = 1 / ρ, unit Ω-1 m-1: it measures how easily a material conducts. Metals have low resistivity; insulators very high.

Worked Example: Potential Difference from Charge Flow

Calculate the potential difference across a wire of resistance 5 Ω if a charge of 720 C passes through it per minute.

Step 1: I = Q / t = 720 / 60 = 12 A.

Step 2: V = I R = 12 x 5 = 60 V.

Answer: 60 V.

Worked Example: Resistivity of a Wire

A 10 m long wire of diameter 0.2 cm has a resistance of 3 Ω. Find the resistivity of its material and its conductivity.

Step 1: Radius r = 0.1 cm = 10-3 m. Area A = π r2 = 3.14 x 10-6 m2.

Step 2: ρ = R A / L = 3 x 3.14 x 10-6 / 10 = 9.4 x 10-7 Ω m.

Step 3: σ = 1 / ρ = 1 / (9.4 x 10-7) = 1.06 x 106 Ω-1 m-1.

Answer: ρ = 9.4 x 10-7 Ω m, σ = 1.06 x 106 Ω-1 m-1.

lessons.title: Effect of Temperature: Thermistor and LDR
lessons.notes_html:
Temperature Coefficient of Resistance

  • Positive coefficient (metals): resistance increases as temperature rises, because the hotter atoms vibrate more and scatter the drifting electrons more often.
  • Negative coefficient (semiconductors, insulators, thermistors): resistance decreases as temperature rises, because heating frees many more charge carriers, and this outweighs the extra scattering.

The Thermistor

A thermistor is a semiconductor device whose resistance changes sharply with temperature; the common type has a negative coefficient, so its resistance falls rapidly as it warms. Uses in daily life:

  • Temperature measurement and control: thermostats and digital thermometers.
  • Fire alarms: a sudden rise in temperature changes the resistance and triggers the alarm.
  • Automatic temperature compensation in circuits, and liquid-level indicators.

The Light Dependent Resistor (LDR)

An LDR is a semiconductor whose resistance decreases when the intensity of light falling on it increases, because the light frees more charge carriers. LDRs are used in automatic street lights, light meters and burglar alarms.

lessons.title: Resistors in Series and Parallel
lessons.notes_html:
Series Connection

The same current flows through every resistor, and the total potential difference is the sum of the separate drops, so the equivalent resistance is the sum:

R = R1 + R2 + R3

  • The series equivalent is always larger than any single resistor in the chain.

Parallel Connection

The same potential difference is across every resistor, and the total current is the sum of the branch currents:

1 / R = 1 / R1 + 1 / R2 + 1 / R3

  • The parallel equivalent is always smaller than the smallest resistor in the group.
  • Household appliances are wired in parallel so that each gets the full supply voltage and can be switched independently.

lessons.title: E.M.F., Internal Resistance and Maximum Power
lessons.notes_html:
The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is the energy it supplies per unit charge; its unit is the volt. A real source also has internal resistance r, inside the source itself.

Terminal voltage V = E - I r

  • While the source delivers current, the terminal voltage is less than the e.m.f. (E is greater than V), because part of the energy is lost across r.
  • When no current is drawn (open circuit, I = 0), the terminal voltage equals the e.m.f. exactly — the only case in which V and E are the same (the ideal limit r = 0 gives it always).

Maximum Power Transfer

A source delivers maximum power to its load when the load resistance equals the internal resistance:

R = r

  • At this point only half of the total power reaches the load; the other half is wasted as heat inside the source, so the efficiency is 50%.

Worked Example: Terminal Voltage

A battery has an e.m.f. of 12.5 V and an internal resistance of 2.4 x 10-3 Ω. If the load current is 20 A, find the terminal voltage.

Step 1: Voltage lost inside the battery = I r = 20 x 2.4 x 10-3 = 0.048 V.

Step 2: V = E - I r = 12.5 - 0.048 = 12.45 V.

Answer: 12.45 V.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's Laws, Wheatstone Bridge and Potentiometer
lessons.notes_html:
Circuit Language

  • A node is a junction where two or more conductors meet and currents divide or combine. A node chosen as the zero-potential reference is called the datum node.
  • A loop is any closed conducting path in the circuit.

Kirchhoff's Laws

  • First law (junction rule): the sum of currents entering a node equals the sum leaving it. It rests on the conservation of charge.
  • Second law (loop rule): around any closed loop, the algebraic sum of e.m.f.s equals the sum of the potential drops. It rests on the conservation of energy.
  • Sign rules: passing through a source from its negative to its positive terminal, E is taken positive; passing through a resistor in the direction of the current, the potential decreases.

Wheatstone Bridge

Four resistors form a diamond, with a galvanometer joining the two middle points. The bridge is balanced when no current flows through the galvanometer:

R1 / R2 = R3 / R4

  • With three known resistors, the fourth (unknown) follows from this condition. Being a null method, it is very accurate.

Potentiometer

A potentiometer measures potential difference and e.m.f. by the null method, drawing no current from the source being measured. A steady current through a uniform wire makes the potential fall uniformly along it; the unknown e.m.f. is balanced against a length of the wire at which the galvanometer shows no deflection. It is used to measure and compare e.m.f.s of cells, to find the internal resistance of a cell, and to calibrate voltmeters and ammeters.

Worked Example: E.M.F. by Potentiometer

The e.m.f. of a battery is balanced by 80 cm of potentiometer wire, while the 1.03 V e.m.f. of a standard cell is balanced by 55 cm. Find the e.m.f. of the battery.

Step 1: E.m.f. is proportional to the balancing length: E = 1.03 x (80 / 55).

Step 2: E = 1.03 x 1.4545 = 1.5 V.

Answer: 1.5 V.

Key Points

  • Coulomb's law: F = k Q1 Q2 / r2 with k = 9 x 109 N m2 C-2; the electron's charge is 1.6 x 10-19 C.
  • Field intensity E = F / q; field lines never cross and give the field direction by their tangent.
  • The field inside a conductor and inside a Faraday cage is zero.
  • Potential V = W / q is a scalar; E = -ΔV / Δd; 1 eV = 1.6 x 10-19 J.
  • A charge entering a uniform field at right angles follows a parabolic path.
  • Current is the drift of charge; in electrolytes and plasmas, ions of both signs carry it.
  • Ohm's law V = I R; resistance R = ρ L / A; conductivity is 1 / ρ.
  • Metals have a positive temperature coefficient; thermistors respond to heat and LDRs to light, both with falling resistance.
  • Series resistances add; parallel reciprocals add.
  • Terminal voltage V = E - I r; maximum power is transferred when R = r.
  • Kirchhoff's first law conserves charge, his second law conserves energy; the Wheatstone bridge balances at R1/R2 = R3/R4.

lessons.title: Magnetic Field of a Current-Carrying Conductor
lessons.notes_html:
A current-carrying conductor is surrounded by a magnetic field. The field lines around a long straight wire are concentric circles centred on the wire.

Right-Hand Grip Rule

Grip the conductor with the right hand, the thumb pointing along the current. The curled fingers then point in the direction of the magnetic field lines circling the conductor.

Field Inside a Solenoid

A solenoid is a long coil of wire. Inside it the field is strong and nearly uniform, like the field of a bar magnet:

B = μ0 n I

  • μ0 — permeability of free space = 4π x 10-7 T m A-1
  • n — number of turns per unit length, I — current

Worked Example: Field Inside a Solenoid

A solenoid 10 cm long has 500 turns. Find the magnetic field inside it when it carries a current of 10 A.

Step 1: n = 500 / 0.10 = 5000 turns per metre.

Step 2: B = μ0 n I = 4π x 10-7 x 5000 x 10 = 4π x 10-7 x 5 x 104.

Answer: B = 6.28 x 10-2 T.

lessons.title: Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor
lessons.notes_html:
A conductor carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences a magnetic force, because the field acts on each of its drifting charge carriers:

F = B I L sin θ

  • B — flux density, I — current, L — length of conductor in the field, θ — angle between the conductor and the field
  • The force is greatest when the conductor is at right angles to the field (θ = 90°) and zero when it is parallel to the field.
  • Its direction is perpendicular to both the field and the conductor, given by Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger Field, second finger Current, thumb Motion (force).

The formula comes from adding the forces q v B sin θ on all the carriers in the length L: with n carriers per unit volume in a wire of cross-section A, the total is F = (n A L) q v B sin θ, and since I = n A q v, this is F = B I L sin θ.

Worked Example: Force on a Conductor

A conductor of length 20 cm carrying a current of 10 A is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 2 T, its length at 60° to the field. Calculate the force on the conductor.

Step 1: F = B I L sin θ = 2 x 10 x 0.20 x sin 60°.

Step 2: sin 60° = 0.866, so F = 4 x 0.866 = 3.46 N.

Answer: F = 3.5 N (approximately).

lessons.title: Force on a Moving Charged Particle
lessons.notes_html:
A single charged particle moving in a magnetic field experiences the force:

F = q v B sin θ

  • The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the particle's direction but never its speed or kinetic energy — a magnetic field does no work on a moving charge.
  • Moving parallel to the field (θ = 0°): no force at all, the particle continues straight.
  • Moving perpendicular to the field (θ = 90°): the force acts as a centripetal force and the particle moves in a circle:

r = m v / (q B)

  • A proton (positive) is deflected in the direction of v x B by Fleming's left-hand rule; an electron (negative) is deflected the opposite way.

Worked Example: Force on a Proton

A proton enters a magnetic field of flux density 1.5 Wb m-2 with a velocity of 2 x 107 m s-1 at an angle of 45° with the field. Compute the force on the proton. (Charge on a proton = 1.6 x 10-19 C.)

Step 1: F = q v B sin θ = 1.6 x 10-19 x 2 x 107 x 1.5 x sin 45°.

Step 2: sin 45° = 0.707, so F = 4.8 x 10-12 x 0.707.

Answer: F = 3.4 x 10-12 N.

Worked Example: Speed of an Electron (Check the Data!)

An electron moves at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.2 T and experiences a force of 2 x 10-2 N. What is its speed?

Step 1: v = F / (e B) = 2 x 10-2 / (1.6 x 10-19 x 0.2) = 2 x 10-2 / 3.2 x 10-20.

Answer: 6.25 x 1017 m s-1 by the arithmetic — but this is faster than the speed of light (3 x 108 m s-1), so the printed data in the book are unphysical; no real electron can reach this speed.

lessons.title: Magnetic Flux and Magnetic Flux Density
lessons.notes_html:
Magnetic flux Φ is the total number of magnetic field lines passing through a surface:

Φ = B A cos θ

  • A — area of the surface, θ — angle between the field and the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface)
  • Flux is maximum when the field is perpendicular to the plane of the area, that is parallel to its normal (θ = 0°, cos θ = 1): Φ = B A.
  • Flux is minimum (zero) when the field lies in the plane of the area (θ = 90°, cos θ = 0).
  • SI unit of flux: the weber (Wb).

Magnetic flux density B is the flux per unit area held normal to the field — it is the strength of the magnetic field itself:

B = Φ / A

  • SI unit: the tesla (T), where 1 T = 1 Wb m-2. In base units, 1 tesla = 1 kg s-2 A-1.
  • The unit of induced e.m.f. is the volt.

lessons.title: Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law
lessons.notes_html:
An induced e.m.f. is the e.m.f. generated in a circuit by a change in the magnetic flux linked with it. Experiments show it clearly: pushing a bar magnet into a coil deflects a galvanometer (and pulling it out deflects it the other way); moving the coil instead of the magnet works just as well; changing the current in a neighbouring coil induces an e.m.f. too; and rotating a coil in a field — the generator — gives a continuously varying e.m.f. In every case the e.m.f. appears only while the flux is changing: a coil and magnet closed together but at rest give zero induced e.m.f.

Faraday's Law (given by Faraday)

ε = - N ΔΦ / Δt

  • The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage; N is the number of turns.

Lenz's Law and the Negative Sign

The negative sign is Lenz's law: the induced e.m.f. and current always act in the direction that opposes the change in flux that produced them. If the flux increases, the induced current makes a field opposing the increase; if the flux decreases, it makes a field supporting it. Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of energy: the electrical energy produced comes from the mechanical work done against this opposition.

Induced E.M.F. versus Induced Current

  • Induced e.m.f. is the cause: the voltage generated by the changing flux. It exists even in an open circuit, as a potential difference across the ends.
  • Induced current is the effect: it flows only when the circuit is closed and the e.m.f. can drive charge around it.

Worked Example: E.M.F. When the Flux Reverses

A coil of 200 turns is linked by a flux of 40 mWb. If this flux is reversed in 4 ms, determine the average induced e.m.f. in the coil.

Step 1: Reversing the flux changes it from +40 mWb to -40 mWb, so ΔΦ = 80 mWb = 0.08 Wb.

Step 2: ε = N ΔΦ / Δt = 200 x 0.08 / 0.004 = 200 x 20.

Answer: 4000 V. (Note: the book prints 2000 V, which is the answer for the flux merely falling to zero; for a full reversal the change is doubled, giving 4000 V.)

lessons.title: Mutual Induction and Self-Induction
lessons.notes_html:
Mutual Induction

Mutual induction is the production of an e.m.f. in one coil by a changing current in a neighbouring coil, through the changing flux that links them:

ε = - M ΔI / Δt

  • M — coefficient of mutual induction (mutual inductance): the e.m.f. induced in the second coil per unit rate of change of current in the first.

Self-Induction

Self-induction is the production of an e.m.f. in a coil by the change of its own current, as its own flux changes:

ε = - L ΔI / Δt

  • L — self-inductance of the coil. By Lenz's law the self-induced e.m.f. opposes the change: it delays the growth of current at switch-on and its decay at switch-off, which is why breaking an inductive circuit produces a spark.

The Henry

One henry (H) is the inductance of a coil in which an e.m.f. of 1 volt is induced when the current changes at 1 ampere per second: 1 H = 1 V s A-1 = 1 Wb A-1. Its dimensions are [M L2 T-2 A-2].

Worked Example: Mutual Inductance

When the current in coil A is increased uniformly from zero to 18 A in 0.3 s, an e.m.f. of 6 V is induced in a nearby coil B. Find the mutual inductance between the coils.

Step 1: Rate of change of current = 18 / 0.3 = 60 A s-1.

Step 2: M = ε / (ΔI / Δt) = 6 / 60 = 0.1 H.

Answer: M = 0.1 H.

Worked Example: Self-Inductance

The current in a coil changes by 3 A in 60 ms, and an e.m.f. of 10 V is induced in the coil. What is its self-inductance?

Step 1: Rate of change of current = 3 / 0.060 = 50 A s-1.

Step 2: L = ε / (ΔI / Δt) = 10 / 50 = 0.2 H.

Answer: L = 0.2 H.

lessons.title: The Transformer
lessons.notes_html:
A transformer changes the voltage of an alternating supply. It works on mutual induction: an alternating current in the primary coil produces a continuously changing flux in the laminated soft-iron core, and this changing flux links the secondary coil and induces an alternating e.m.f. in it. The soft iron core enhances the magnetic flux and guides it from one coil to the other. A transformer works only with A.C., because a steady current produces no changing flux.

Vs / Vp = Ns / Np

  • Step-up transformer: Ns greater than Np, so the voltage rises and the current falls. Used at power stations so electricity can be transmitted at high voltage.
  • Step-down transformer: Ns less than Np, so the voltage falls and the current rises. Used near consumers to deliver safe voltages such as 220 V.
  • An ideal transformer wastes nothing: input power = output power.
  • For long-distance transmission we use a smaller current and a higher voltage, because the heating loss in the lines is I2 R and falls rapidly as the current is reduced.

Power Losses in a Real Transformer

  • Copper losses: I2 R heating in the windings.
  • Eddy current losses: circulating currents induced in the core — reduced by laminating the core.
  • Hysteresis losses: energy lost in repeatedly magnetizing and demagnetizing the core — reduced by using soft iron.
  • Flux leakage: flux that links only one coil — reduced by winding the coils close together on the same core.

Worked Example: Turns on a Step-Down Transformer

A step-down transformer is used on a 1 kV line to deliver 220 V. How many turns are on the primary winding if the secondary has 50 turns?

Step 1: Np / Ns = Vp / Vs, so Np = 50 x (1000 / 220).

Step 2: Np = 50 x 4.545 = 227.3.

Answer: about 227 turns on the primary.

Key Points

  • The field around a straight current is concentric circles; find its direction with the right-hand grip rule.
  • Force on a conductor: F = B I L sin θ, direction by Fleming's left-hand rule.
  • Force on a moving charge: F = q v B sin θ; it does no work, and a charge crossing the field at right angles moves in a circle of radius m v / (q B).
  • Flux Φ = B A cos θ (unit weber); flux density B = Φ / A (unit tesla).
  • Faraday's law: ε = - N ΔΦ / Δt; the negative sign is Lenz's law, which follows from conservation of energy.
  • Induced e.m.f. exists in an open circuit; induced current needs a closed circuit.
  • Mutual inductance M and self-inductance L are both measured in henries.
  • A transformer works on mutual induction with A.C. only: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np.
  • Transmit power at high voltage and low current to cut I2 R losses.

lessons.title: Relative Motion and Frames of Reference
lessons.notes_html:
Relative motion is the motion of a body as observed from a particular frame of reference: the same motion looks different to different observers.

  • A passenger sitting in a moving train is at rest for a fellow passenger, but in motion for an observer standing on the platform.
  • Raindrops fall vertically, yet appear to fall slanting to a person walking through the rain.
  • Two cars moving in the same direction at the same speed are at rest relative to each other, while a car coming the opposite way appears to move with the sum of the two speeds.

Inertial and Non-Inertial Frames

  • An inertial frame is at rest or moving with uniform velocity (no acceleration). Newton's laws hold in it in their simple form.
  • A non-inertial frame is accelerated or rotating. In it, fictitious forces such as centrifugal force appear, and Newton's laws need correction terms.

lessons.title: Special Theory of Relativity
lessons.notes_html:
Einstein's special theory of relativity (1905) rests on two postulates:

  • All the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference.
  • The speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer.

Its Main Consequences

  • Relativity of simultaneity: events that are simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another.
  • Length contraction: a moving object is measured shorter along its direction of motion:

L = L0 √(1 - v2 / c2)

  • Time dilation: a moving clock runs slow:

T = T0 / √(1 - v2 / c2)

  • Mass variation: the mass of a moving object increases:

m = m0 / √(1 - v2 / c2)

  • Mass-energy equivalence:

E = m c2

E0 = m0 c2

  • E0 — rest energy of a body of rest mass m0
  • Space-time is described with four coordinates, the fourth being x4 = i c t.
  • A particle can travel at the speed of light only if its rest mass is zero, like the photon: for any massive particle the mass would become infinite at v = c, needing infinite energy, so massive particles always stay below c.

lessons.title: Relativistic Effects: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example: Length Contraction

How fast must a rocket go for its length to be contracted to 80% of its rest length?

Step 1: L / L0 = 0.80 = √(1 - v2 / c2). Squaring: 0.64 = 1 - v2 / c2.

Step 2: v2 / c2 = 1 - 0.64 = 0.36, so v = 0.6 c.

Answer: v = 0.6 x 3 x 108 = 1.8 x 108 m s-1.

Worked Example: Time Dilation

The period of a seconds pendulum is 2 s in its own frame. What period does an observer measure who moves at 0.9 c relative to the pendulum's frame?

Step 1: T = T0 / √(1 - v2 / c2) = 2 / √(1 - 0.81) = 2 / √0.19.

Step 2: √0.19 = 0.436, so T = 2 / 0.436 = 4.6 s.

Answer: 4.6 s — the moving observer sees the pendulum swinging more slowly.

Worked Example: Relativistic Mass

Calculate the mass of an object of rest mass m0 moving at 0.85 c.

Step 1: m = m0 / √(1 - 0.852) = m0 / √(1 - 0.7225) = m0 / √0.2775.

Step 2: √0.2775 = 0.527, so m = m0 / 0.527.

Answer: m = 1.9 m0 — the mass is nearly doubled.

lessons.title: Discovery of the Fundamental Particles and Accelerators
lessons.notes_html:
A Brief History

  • 1897: the electron, discovered by Thomson — the first fundamental particle.
  • 1917: the proton, identified by Rutherford.
  • 1932: the neutron (Chadwick), and the positron — the first antiparticle discovered (the antielectron), predicted by Dirac and found by Anderson in cosmic rays.
  • Cosmic-ray studies then revealed the muon, the pion and the kaons.
  • 1964: the quark model of Gell-Mann and Zweig explained hadrons as combinations of quarks.
  • 1983: the W and Z bosons found at CERN; 1995: the top quark; 2012: the Higgs boson, completing the Standard Model's particle list.

Cosmic Rays

Cosmic rays are highly energetic particles — mostly protons and atomic nuclei — arriving at the Earth from outer space. Their sources are violent events: the Sun, supernova explosions in our galaxy, and still more energetic sources beyond it such as active galactic nuclei and gamma-ray bursts. Entering the atmosphere, they collide with air nuclei and produce showers of secondary particles.

Particle Accelerators

A particle accelerator accelerates charged particles to very high speeds and energies with electric fields, while magnetic fields steer and focus the beam. Types include linear accelerators and circular machines (cyclotrons, synchrotrons and the Large Hadron Collider). Their uses:

  • Probing the structure of matter and discovering new particles.
  • Producing radioisotopes for medical diagnosis and cancer therapy.
  • Materials testing and sterilization.
  • Industrial uses such as ion implantation in semiconductors.

lessons.title: Particles and Antiparticles
lessons.notes_html:
Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass and lifetime but opposite charge and opposite values of the other additive quantum numbers (baryon number, lepton number and so on).

  • Electron and positron (antielectron) — the first antiparticle discovered.
  • Proton and antiproton; neutron and antineutron.
  • When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate each other and their mass appears as gamma-ray photons.

Matter-Antimatter Asymmetry

The universe contains far more matter than antimatter, although the Big Bang should have made them in equal amounts. This baryon asymmetry — an imbalance in the number of baryons — is an unsolved mystery: the known CP violation in weak interactions is far too small to explain it, so some process in the very early universe must have favoured matter by about one part in a billion. The surviving excess is all the matter we see; the rest annihilated into radiation.

The Strong Nuclear Force

The strong nuclear force is the short-range attractive force that holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus, overcoming their electrostatic repulsion. It is the strongest of the four forces at its range. Between quarks it is mediated by gluons — massless particles that themselves carry colour charge and bind quarks inside protons, neutrons and other hadrons. The force felt between nucleons is a residual effect of this gluon exchange, carried between nucleons by pions.

Electroweak Unification

At very high energies the electromagnetic and weak forces are two aspects of a single electroweak interaction, mediated by one set of bosons (photon, W+, W- and Z). At ordinary energies the symmetry is broken by the Higgs mechanism, so the forces appear different: electromagnetism is long-ranged, the weak force very short-ranged.

lessons.title: Quarks, Leptons, Fermions and Bosons
lessons.notes_html:
Quarks

There are six types (flavours) of quark in three generations: (up, down), (charm, strange) and (top, bottom). Ordinary matter is built only from up and down quarks; the heavier flavours appear in high-energy collisions and decay quickly.

  • Baryons are formed by a combination of three quarks (proton = uud, neutron = udd).
  • Mesons are formed by a quark and an antiquark.
  • A neutron is converted into a proton when it absorbs a π+ or emits a π- — the charge balances in both cases.

Strange Particles

Strange particles contain a strange quark. They are produced in pairs by the strong interaction (associated production) but decay slowly by the weak interaction — a puzzling combination that earned them their name and led to the strangeness quantum number. Examples: the K-mesons (kaons) and the lambda hyperon.

Leptons

There are six leptons in three generations: the electron, muon and tau, with their three neutrinos (electron, muon and tau neutrinos). Leptons do not feel the strong force; charged leptons feel the electromagnetic and weak forces, while neutrinos feel only the weak force and gravity.

Fermions and Bosons

  • Fermions: half-integral spin (1/2, 3/2, ...). They obey the Pauli exclusion principle — no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state. Quarks and leptons are fermions; electrons, protons and neutrons are fermions.
  • Bosons: zero or integral spin (0, 1, 2, ...). They do not obey the exclusion principle and can share states. Photons, gluons and the Higgs boson are bosons — the force carriers.

lessons.title: Alpha, Beta and Gamma Radiations
lessons.notes_html:

Alpha radiation is heavily ionizing; gamma radiation is the most penetrating. Gamma rays are emitted with discrete energies when a nucleus drops from an excited state.

Why Alpha Energies Are Discrete but Beta Energies Continuous

  • Alpha decay is a two-body decay between two definite nuclear energy levels: the energy is shared by only the alpha particle and the recoiling daughter nucleus, so every alpha particle from that decay carries nearly the same, discrete energy.
  • Beta decay is a three-body decay: the energy is shared among the daughter nucleus, the electron and an antineutrino, so the electron takes a continuous range of energies up to a maximum — the missing energy carried away by the antineutrino, as Pauli proposed to save energy conservation.

Beta-Minus Decay in Detail

In beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a proton (a proton changing into a neutron is beta-plus decay):

n → p + e- + anti-νe

  • At the quark level, a down quark changes into an up quark by emitting a W- boson, which decays into the electron and the antineutrino.
  • Charge, baryon number and lepton number are all conserved.

Conservation Laws in Reactions and Decays

Every particle reaction or decay must conserve: energy (including mass-energy), linear momentum, angular momentum, electric charge, baryon number, lepton number for each generation, and colour charge. Strangeness is conserved in strong and electromagnetic processes but not in weak decays. A proposed reaction is possible only if it satisfies all of these laws.

lessons.title: The Higgs Boson, Plasma and String Theory
lessons.notes_html:
The Higgs Boson and Mass

The Higgs boson is the quantum of the Higgs field, which fills all space, and it is the particle responsible for the mass of the elementary particles. Particles gain mass by interacting with this field: those that interact strongly (like the top quark) are heavy, those that interact weakly (like the electron) are light, and those that do not interact at all (like the photon) stay massless. The Higgs boson itself — the observable excitation of the field, discovered at CERN in 2012 — confirms the mechanism, which also gives mass to the W and Z bosons.

Most Matter in the Universe Is Plasma

Plasma, the fourth state of matter, is an ionized gas of free electrons and ions. Stars are balls of plasma, and the space between stars and galaxies is filled with extremely dilute plasma; the early universe was plasma too. By mass, the solid, liquid and gaseous matter on planets is only a tiny fraction of the universe's ordinary matter — the overwhelming bulk exists as plasma in stars and interstellar space.

String Theory

String theory proposes that the fundamental objects are tiny one-dimensional strings rather than point particles. In its consistent form it requires 10 dimensions of space-time — far more than the four we experience.

Key Points

  • Motion is relative to a frame of reference; Newton's laws hold simply only in inertial frames.
  • Relativity: the laws of physics and the speed of light are the same for all inertial observers.
  • Moving lengths contract, moving clocks run slow, moving masses increase; E = m c2.
  • Only a particle of zero rest mass can travel at the speed of light.
  • First antiparticle found: the positron (antielectron), 1932.
  • Four interactions: strong (gluons), electromagnetic (photon), weak (W and Z bosons), gravitational (weakest).
  • Six quarks and six leptons, in three generations; baryons are three quarks, mesons a quark and an antiquark.
  • Fermions have half-integral spin and obey Pauli's principle; bosons have integral spin and carry the forces.
  • Beta-minus decay turns a neutron into a proton; alpha energies are discrete, beta energies continuous.
  • The Higgs boson gives elementary particles their mass; most matter in the universe is plasma.
